html.4本の帰り道に黄色い点が戻り、車体の板を通ってバッテリーのマイナス端子へ帰ってい: The yellow dots are back on the four return paths, going through the body sheet to the battery's negative terminal. The ground isn't something that's fine "as long as it's attached"; it's a path every bit as important as the outbound one. Many electrical problems on classic cars are on this side, not the positive side.
html.500 のアースは、部品ごとに<b>車体（ボディ）へ落ちて</b>います。落とす: On the 500, each part goes to ground on the body separately. Where it goes is the steel panel right next to that part.
html.<b>アースを直す作業では、必ずバッテリーのマイナス（−）端子を最初に外してくだ:
When working on grounds, always disconnect the battery's negative (−) terminal first. Re-tightening a ground means your spanner touches the body (= negative). With the positive side still live, the moment a tool on the battery's positive (+) terminal touches the body, enough current flows to burn the tool. Negative off first, negative back on last.
⚠️ If you scrape off paint to clean a ground terminal, apply rust protection (grease or paint) after tightening. Bare steel rusts, and the same symptom comes back.
html.<b>キーON＝2つの警告灯が点いている。</b>その電気は、ダイナモのマイナス: Key ON = both warning lights lit. Their current goes to the body at two places, the dynamo's negative terminal and the oil pressure sender, and travels through the body back to the battery's negative terminal. The yellow dots move upwards because they are "going home".
html.<b>レバーを引く＝セルが回る。</b>セルの帰り道（一番上の太い線）にも黄色い: Pull the lever = the starter turns. Yellow dots now flow on the starter's return path too (the heavy line at the top). The outbound paths are separate for each part, but the return paths all meet in this one sheet.
html.<span class=\"pin-sub\">●</span>セル・<span: ● Starter, ● regulator, ● oil pressure sender, and the dynamo — their grounds are all in the engine bay. But the ● battery is at the front of the car (in the trunk). So the return path runs from one end of the car to the other through the body steel itself. Break the continuity anywhere in the steel between back and front, and that alone kills everything.
html.<span class=\"qa-h\">先に断っておくこと</span> <b: A caveat first If it's "dim or weak" rather than "doesn't light", this diagram has no answer. On real cars, the most common form of a bad ground is actually not a complete break but a "narrowing" (rusty terminals, paint caught under them). This diagram only calculates connected or not; it has no notion of how "narrow" a path is. Dim headlights, a starter that turns weakly — symptoms like these come out as "normal" here. Judging them needs real voltage measurement (see "what this diagram doesn't have" below).
html.<span class=\"qa-h\">車体に落としてあっても、アースになって: Grounded to the body doesn't always mean grounded It's only a ground if the panel it goes to connects all the way to the battery's negative terminal. If paint, sealer, rust or rubber bushes break the continuity, that panel is not a ground. On cars with bodywork or repairs, this really does get broken.
html.⚠️<b>オルタネーターに換えた車には、外付けのレギュレータがありません。</b: ⚠️ Cars converted to an alternator have no separate regulator. The regulator ground that went to the body on the original is gone, and the charging grounds are gathered at the alternator's own mounting (bolted to the engine). When reading "only the charge lamp doesn't light" in the table above, look at the alternator's mounting bolts and bracket instead of the dynamo's fittings (some conversions run a separate ground wire, so following the wires on your own car by eye is the surest way). The ● regulator in the diagrams further on is also a part converted cars don't have. Grounds of parts on the engine finally return through the ground strap to the battery's negative terminal — the shape of this return path is the same on converted cars. The charging side of converted cars has its own story in the Part 1 extra, "The charge lamp won't go out: alternator conversion".

The ground comes right after the bulb; wires and switches come after that.
